result:
I think a lot about thresholds. Not the big, cinematic ones — graduations, weddings, moving across the country — but the small, unnoticed doors we step through every day. The moment you decide to get out of bed before the second alarm. The second you choose to wave to a neighbor instead of looking away. The quiet click when a difficult idea finally makes sense after reading a paragraph three times.

We love stories about overnight transformations, but most lives change in increments so tiny they would be invisible if you weren't paying attention. A houseplant that was drooping perks up two days after watering. A friendship deepens not because of one long conversation, but because of a hundred brief check-ins. A skill — guitar, coding, cooking — goes from impossible to automatic through repetition that feels boring while it's happening.

Maybe that's why I like trains. You sit still and the world moves, but really you are moving too, just smoothly enough that you don't feel the acceleration. If you stare out the window, the foreground blurs, but the distant mountains stay steady.

If you're in a blurry foreground right now, it might help to look further out. Progress isn't always loud. Sometimes it's just staying on the track long enough for the scenery to finally change. 

That is a modest kind of hope, but it is durable. It does not ask you to be extraordinary, only to continue. And continuation, practiced daily, is quietly extraordinary itself.
